video_title: How Top Prop Traders Find and Scale Their Edge · Jeff Holden
gist: Jeff Holden, head of trader development at SMB Capital, lays out the firm's full system for building professional discretionary traders: a percentage-based 'ASSET' risk-allocation protocol, a baseline-scalping-first curriculum with a measured four-month consistency tipping point before risk is increased, and a live dissection (with host Kevin) of a real CAR/Avis Budget Group short-squeeze trade that shows how the disposition effect quietly caps winners.

insights.claim: SMB Capital's traders size every trade using a fixed percentage-of-daily-stop allocation scale: A+ setups get 80% of the daily stop, A setups get 30%, B setups get 15%, and C (baseline) setups get only 5%, with traders expected to refine these numbers as they gain experience.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A concrete, transferable position-sizing template: tie size to a graded conviction score (A+/A/B/C) rather than to gut feel or P&L, so risk scales with true opportunity quality.
insights.quote: A+ which is 80% of a daily stop, A which is 30% of a daily stop, B which is 15% of a daily stop or C which is 5% of a daily stop.

insights.claim: The firm's trade-execution checklist is deliberately ordered as Allocation, Stop, Entry, Target (ASSET) — stop is set immediately after allocation and before entry is even considered, because pre-committing to 'where I'm wrong' strips the emotional charge out of the trade before it's live.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Sequencing the risk decision before the entry decision is a mechanical fix for the classic problem of traders anchoring their stop to hope instead of invalidation logic.
insights.quote: That stop takes away a lot of the psychological pressures because if you've already accepted the risk and knowing where you're wrong... it's really hard to let the emotions win at that point.

insights.claim: The ASSET protocol went through four or five earlier acronym versions before settling on its current form; the key correction from the earlier versions was moving the stop-setting step from near the end of the process to right after allocation, second overall.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Even a firm's flagship framework was iterated multiple times — a reminder that a trading process should be treated as a live system to keep refining, not a one-time rulebook.

insights.claim: Target-setting is deliberately kept simple and static for developing traders: one or two measured moves off the setup's range, treated as a self-fulfilling target rather than something to over-engineer.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Removes a common source of overtrading/second-guessing — a fixed, rule-based target lets a developing trader test whether they can even execute a base strategy before adding discretionary trade management.
insights.quote: It should move one measured move for a range break. We often talk about a measured move or two measured moves of the range... That's all it is, right? That's all we do.

insights.claim: Career success is framed as the equation 'Baseline + A+ = Career': a trader first needs a repeatable baseline of scalping strategies generating steady income (e.g., ~$5,000/month), which then creates the capital and psychological runway to swing hard at rare, highly telegraphed A+ opportunities.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Reframes 'find your edge' advice: durability comes from a boring, repeatable base rate, not from chasing home runs — the home runs are an overlay on top of a working baseline, not a substitute for one.
insights.quote: A plus plus B, you know, of your baseline equals a trading career.

insights.claim: New traders should build a single validated setup+trade combination first (e.g., a specific range-break-into-opening-range-break pattern) and only slowly scale risk on it (e.g., from risking $50 to $70, or $100 to $200) before adding more strategies; the firm's internal data shows the goal should be five working strategies, but rushing to five before mastering one is a common failure mode.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A staged strategy-building roadmap (1 → 3 → 5 strategies) investors/traders can use to sequence their own skill development rather than diversifying prematurely.
insights.quote: Once you've built one, then the goal is to get to three and then to five. And if you're at five, that's where we really see traders have that sustainability.

insights.claim: The commonly cited rule that '90% of profits come from 10% of trades' is statistically true over a full trading career but is actively misleading for a developing trader, because it tempts them to fixate on hunting big winners (and to size up prematurely) instead of building consistency first.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A widely repeated trading maxim should be applied differently depending on career stage — evaluate any 'edge' aphorism against the specific stage of the trader/strategy before acting on it.
insights.quote: That's a very accurate statement over your trading career for most people, but it's a somewhat misleading statement as a developing trader.

insights.claim: Internal firm data on traders 'coming up the curve' showed a tipping point at four months of sustained consistency — not the two months the firm originally assumed — after which increasing a trader's daily stop produced exponential (not linear) P&L growth, because the trader had built durable 'consistency muscle memory' first.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A measurable, testable heuristic for capital allocators or self-directed traders: don't increase size/risk based on a short hot streak — wait for a data-validated consistency threshold (here, roughly a full quarter) before scaling.
insights.quote: What we found was there was a tipping point at month four... it became this really exponential growth curve.

insights.claim: Traders who show one month of consistency and then lose it effectively get reset in their development timeline, as if the clock restarts — reinforcing that the firm treats a single month of good performance as noise, not a signal to increase risk.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Confirms that short-run track records (even a full profitable month) are unreliable signals for capital allocation decisions in discretionary trading.
insights.quote: Traders that would show consistency for one month and then lose that consistency. It was almost like they got set back in time until they started to get that consistency back.

insights.claim: SMB Capital deliberately starts all new traders on high-repetition scalping strategies rather than swing/position trades, because scalping provides the fastest rep count for building a reliable baseline and gives traders something to fall back on in months when no A+ setup appears.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Explains a specific, structural reason (rep velocity, not just 'start small') for why prop desks train juniors on scalps before bigger discretionary trades — transferable to any trader designing their own onboarding curriculum.
insights.quote: Scalping offered us a structural way to teach and allow our traders to learn consistently. They were able to get a lot of reps in so they could learn very quickly.

insights.claim: Report-card data reviewed across multiple trader cohorts showed that what sustained traders' careers year after year was their baseline/C-level trades, not their A+ trades — the big trades get the attention, but the boring trades keep traders in business.
insights.speaker: host / Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Empirically supports weighting trader evaluation (and personal trading review) toward consistency of base-rate strategies rather than home-run trades.

themes.theme: Reading the Tape and the Bell Fade Setup

insights.claim: SMB Capital's trader-development team has doubled down on teaching tape reading (time & sales / level 2) even as many market participants say it 'doesn't work anymore' post-fragmentation, because it still reveals the real-time interplay of aggressive buyers vs. passive/lazy sellers that a chart pattern alone can't show.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Against the popular narrative that tape reading is obsolete due to fragmented liquidity/algos, a live prop desk still treats it as core edge — worth re-examining for anyone who dismissed it as a legacy-era skill.
insights.quote: We've actually gone deeper and deeper into reading the tape throughout the time that I've been leading the trader development.

insights.claim: Two charts that look nearly identical on a 1-5 minute timeframe can have completely different tape signatures — one showing aggressive buyers stepping up and holding (a real buy program) and the other showing buyers stepping up but then getting 'rug pulled,' meaning identical chart patterns are not equivalent trades and must be filtered through tape context, not price pattern alone.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A concrete argument against pure chart-pattern trading: the same visual setup can be a high-edge trade or a trap depending on order-flow context invisible on the chart.
insights.quote: Even though the charts in the five minute or the one minute or the two-minute look very similar, when you're reading the tape, you're really hearing the story... of the interplay between the buyers and the sellers.

insights.claim: The 'Bell fade' (named after trader Mike Bell/'Bella') is a specific long setup: a stock gaps up more than 3% on genuine good news with elevated pre-market volume, then a 'lazy' seller (not fighting for price, just dumping) drives it down hard off the open despite what should be strong institutional buying support; the trade is to buy as soon as that lazy seller lifts (visible on tape), with a stop just below the low of day.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A fully specified, replicable intraday long setup with explicit entry trigger (seller exhaustion on tape) and stop logic (low of day) that a discretionary trader could paper-test.
insights.quote: It's a lazy cell program that just is selling selling selling. Not even trying to fight for price at all... as soon as that seller lifted, it was almost like it was like the end of that sell program would happen.

insights.claim: SMB Capital distinguishes 'tape scalping' (using the tape for both entry and exit, a hard skill prone to false confidence when market conditions/participants shift) from 'price action scalping' (using tape-confirmed, structurally repeatable patterns with defined expected behavior through the whole trade) — new traders are taught the latter first because it comes with a clear roadmap of what should happen at each stage.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A useful taxonomy for self-assessing one's own scalping style: pure tape scalping requires an edge that degrades fast as market structure changes, while price-action scalping is more teachable and repeatable for developing traders.
insights.quote: Price action scalping is different than tape scalping. Price action scalping has structure to it and it has usually very repeatable historical patterns that you can observe.

insights.claim: SMB Capital uses a 'shot clock' concept (borrowed from basketball) for every trade: there's a reasonable window in which the market should confirm the thesis (expected value should start increasing); if that window passes with the stock doing nothing, expected value is deemed to be diminishing and the trader must reassess, even though the hard stop hasn't been hit.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Adds a time-based invalidation layer on top of price-based stops — useful for traders whose stop-loss discipline is fine but who bleed time/opportunity cost sitting in dead trades.
insights.quote: Your job in fact is to understand when the market is going to move in your favor and then enter the trade. Not enter the trade and then hope it moves in my favor.

insights.claim: New traders are explicitly NOT taught to actively manage the shot-clock/time-based adjustment early on, because it adds a variable that's too advanced before basic stop discipline is mastered — beginners are told to simply take the signal, size small, and manage risk only, deferring reward management.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A sequencing lesson applicable beyond trading: master the base risk-control skill before layering discretionary refinements on top, or the refinements just add noise.
insights.quote: Just make sure you actually have the rules for your trade present. And if you have them, put the trade on and manage your risk. Don't worry about managing your reward quite yet.

themes.theme: Managing Winners: The CAR/Avis Short-Squeeze Case Study

insights.claim: Host Kevin shorted Avis Budget Group (ticker CAR) on what he identified as a textbook 'first red day' fade of an overextended move, correctly waiting for the actual signal rather than pre-shorting on the way up — but the position was managed so conservatively (taking quarters off into the first down leg) that he captured roughly only a fifth of the total available move before the stock reversed hard.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin)
insights.so_what: A real, dated case study (CAR short-squeeze unwind) of correct setup identification undermined by premature profit-taking — illustrates that trade ID is necessary but not sufficient; trade management determines realized P&L.
insights.quote: This thing goes from $800 to $200 that day... and I don't take advantage of it at all because this disposition effect.

insights.claim: During the CAR squeeze, market chatter circulated claims of 127%–140% of the float being short, fueling speculation the stock could run to $1,000–$5,000; Jeff notes the stock traded with unusually poor liquidity/participation on the way up, which made many traders (including some at SMB) genuinely afraid of it rather than confident.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified account of the float/short-interest narrative that accompanied one of the year's most extreme single-stock squeezes — useful context for anyone modeling squeeze mechanics or researching this specific move.
insights.quote: People started circulating those stories about the floats being locked and 140% short float or 127% short float and like all these stories that everybody's like this could go to a thousand, this could go to 5,000.

insights.claim: Jeff's framework for judging whether an extended squeeze is 'getting better or getting worse' (i.e., safe to fade vs. dangerous to fight) is participation/liquidity quality, not just price direction — he contrasts CAR (got worse, then rapidly got better/healthier before the eventual reversal) with HKD, a stock he cites as an 'awful example' that kept getting worse and worse as it rose, making it dangerous to short into strength.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A risk filter for anyone shorting or fading momentum/squeeze stocks: track order-flow quality and participation breadth, not just how extended price looks, before sizing a countertrend trade.
insights.quote: HKD was an awful example of it before where as it went higher it actually got worse and worse and worse... this one was one that was really interesting because it got worse and worse and worse and then better and better and better really really fast.

insights.claim: A trader who correctly identifies a setup like CAR but gets stopped out on full size should not treat that loss as proof the strategy is wrong — Jeff frames a properly-sized loss taken within risk controls as simply the cost of being a trader, not a signal to blacklist the ticker or the setup after one failed attempt.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Guards against a common behavioral error (abandoning a correctly-identified edge after one loss) — the diagnostic question should be whether the setup criteria were truly met, not whether the single trade won.
insights.quote: I tried it once. It was exactly what I wanted to see. I got stopped out on big size. That sucks. But didn't you sign up for this as a trader, right?

insights.claim: In the CAR squeeze, the true A+ confirmation signal (three consecutive gap-ups with acceleration away from a moving average, acceleration outside a Bollinger Band, and accelerating volume — several of these occurring together for the first time) didn't actually appear until later in the move than most traders assumed, meaning many people mislabeled early stages of the move as A+ when they weren't yet.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable multi-factor confirmation stack (consecutive gaps + moving-average/Bollinger-Band acceleration + volume acceleration) for distinguishing a genuinely climactic move from one that merely looks extended.
insights.quote: There were all these characteristics that were there for the first time that most of us would identify as pivotal for an A+ opportunity that really didn't show up until later in the trade.

insights.claim: SMB Capital enforces two hard emotional-discipline rules: a loss may be mourned for a maximum of 24 hours before the trader must return to trading mode, and a win may be celebrated for a maximum of 12 hours before the same reset applies — the asymmetry (losses get double the processing time) is treated as a deliberate, learned rule, not arbitrary.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A simple, adoptable discipline rule for any trader to bound the emotional 'hangover' (positive or negative) from a single trade so it doesn't bleed into the next session's decision-making.
insights.quote: You can only mourn a loss for 24 hours... You can only celebrate a win for 12 hours.

insights.claim: The 'disposition effect' (being fearful when a trade is winning and hopeful when it's losing) is identified by the host as the direct cause of exiting the CAR short too early — he took a quarter off on the very first down move, which Jeff argues psychologically shifted him into 'retreat mode' for the rest of the trade even though logically the position was working as expected.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin) / Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Names the specific mechanical trigger (taking an early partial) that converts a trader from aggressor to defender mid-trade — suggests reviewing exactly when/why partials are taken as a lever to fix under-sizing winners.
insights.quote: As soon as your mind goes into profit taking, it really is hard and you have to be very conscious of no, no, no, this is an opportunity to stay the aggressor.

insights.claim: Jeff identifies three distinct trader archetypes for managing a working position, each requiring different internal self-talk: (1) 'adders' who keep adding/raising stops and must tell themselves 'it's okay if I lose it all, I'll win big if it works'; (2) 'core-capture' traders who exit into strength and must tell themselves 'I caught the meat of the move, I don't need the rest'; and (3) 'forced-out aggressors' who hold a full position without adding until stopped out, telling themselves 'they have to rip these shares out of my hands' — counterintuitively, the third group's self-talk is the most aggressive despite looking the most passive.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Gives traders a diagnostic to identify which archetype they naturally are (or want to become) and match trade-management tactics and self-talk accordingly, rather than copying a strategy that fights their psychology.
insights.quote: That last voice typically is the most aggressive voice, right? The one that they need to take these shares out of my hand. I'm going to make them beat me.

insights.claim: Jeff explicitly calls passion for markets 'overrated' as a predictive signal of trading success — he has observed many people who are intensely passionate fans of trading/markets who never develop real edge, comparing it to sports fans who are passionate about a team without being able to play for it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a common self-selection narrative ('I love markets, so I'll be a good trader') — investors evaluating traders (or themselves) should weight for positive expectancy behaviors over enthusiasm.
insights.quote: I think passion's overrated... I've seen intensely passionate people about the markets that never really explore edge. They're just really big fans of trading.

insights.claim: The traits SMB Capital actually screens for in the hiring/interview process are competitiveness, diligence, and equanimity — diligence in particular is described as underrated relative to its actual importance.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A concrete hiring/self-assessment checklist for what actually predicts trading success at a professional prop desk, as opposed to commonly assumed traits like raw enthusiasm or intelligence.
insights.quote: I would say that competitiveness is one of them. Diligence is one of them... equanimity we think is very important.

insights.claim: When outside researchers (from universities or PE-funded firms) have proposed studying SMB Capital's top traders to find personality commonalities, the firm's internal view is skeptical — their best traders are successful precisely because of their differences, not shared traits, and forcing a single personality template would produce a diluted 'worst of both worlds' composite rather than useful insight.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Cautions against building a single 'ideal trader profile' for hiring or self-improvement — individualized strength-based development may be more productive than trying to match a composite template.
insights.quote: The reason why I think every person that I've ever met that's been successful in markets, the reason for their success is because they're bringing themselves into the market.

insights.claim: Jeff endorses trader Michael Marcus's observation that combining two of the best traders would produce the worst of both, connecting it to the idea that trading strategy must be congruent with individual personality rather than copied wholesale from even a top performer.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden / (attributed to Michael Marcus)
insights.so_what: Reinforces that mimicking a successful trader's exact style without personality fit is likely to underperform both the original strategies — supports personalized rather than copy-paste strategy adoption.
insights.quote: If you take two of the best traders and combine them you'll get the worst from both of them.

insights.claim: Jeff frames AI as unlikely to 'take over' discretionary trading; instead he expects a wave of 'AI slop' to muck up markets somewhat, which he views as net additive to opportunity for skilled human/discretionary traders rather than a threat, because inefficiency (however sourced) is what a discretionary edge exploits.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A specific, contrarian-adjacent prediction about AI's market-structure effect: rather than compressing discretionary edge, more AI-driven noise/participation may widen the opportunity set for pattern-based human traders.
insights.quote: This is why I think some people say AI is going to take over trading. I don't see that actually happening. I see a lot of AI slop coming into the market... that's going to tend to create opportunity for us more than anything else.

insights.claim: Jeff personally uses AI tools (naming Claude specifically) to compress research that used to take teams of people hours into roughly 5–10 minutes of work, and notes a trader could go further and build an autonomous research agent that runs overnight.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A live example of a professional trading desk already using LLMs for research workflow compression — signals where discretionary trading operations are heading operationally, even while human judgment stays central to execution.
insights.quote: We have Claude to help us with all of these things that we can do research that used to take teams of people hours and hours and hours of doing. I can do by myself in 10 minutes.

insights.claim: Jeff traces his own drive for trading independence to a formative childhood experience: his father lost his job when an entire department was cut, and the family lost access to their neighborhood community pool as a direct consequence — this shaped Jeff's core belief that he wants full personal control over whether he wins or loses, rather than being exposed to decisions outside his control.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Illustrates a recurring pattern among successful discretionary traders: a formative loss-of-control experience often underlies the drive toward a career built on direct personal accountability for outcomes.
insights.quote: I don't want to ever be in a position where I'm completely exposed... If I lose, I want it to be because of me. And also, if I win, I want it to because be because of me.

insights.claim: 80% of developing traders need to be actively pushed by their mentors to put on more risk when a genuine A+ opportunity appears, rather than being naturally inclined to size up — most people's default psychological wiring under-sizes their best opportunities.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A striking base rate: the binding constraint on most developing traders' returns is not finding edge but psychologically permitting themselves to size into it — a specific, measurable coaching target.
insights.quote: You'll have traders come in that are developing and you've noticed that 80% of them need to be pushed to put risk [on].

themes.theme: Team Trading, Community, and Firm Structure

insights.claim: SMB Capital distinguishes 'community trading' (traders sharing ideas but executing independently) from 'team trading' (traders sharing an actual common playbook and coordinated execution) — the firm only began building formal team-trading structures around 2019, and considers a shared playbook the defining structural test of whether a group is a real team or just a community.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A clear operational distinction for traders considering forming or joining a trading group: sharing ideas casually is a lesser (though still valuable) structure than committing to one shared, disciplined playbook.
insights.quote: If you had a team that wasn't on the same playbook, would they be a very good team in any sport anywhere? They probably wouldn't.

insights.claim: As teams mature under SMB's model, they progress toward what Jeff calls 'pack hunting' — coordinated, heightened-intensity focus on the best shared opportunities, analogous to a sports team's noticeably tighter preparation before a big game versus a routine practice.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Suggests that mature trading teams should deliberately ramp collective intensity/coordination around their highest-conviction (A+) opportunities rather than applying uniform effort across all trades.

insights.claim: SMB Capital deliberately runs a mentoring model with multiple mentors rather than a single mentor per trader, on the premise that a developing trader absorbing partial lessons from several experienced traders and synthesizing them personally produces better outcomes than following one person's complete style.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: An organizational design choice for trading education/mentorship programs — diversify mentor exposure rather than pairing a trainee with a single senior trader long-term.
insights.quote: On our desk, mentoring is not a one-person thing. You don't have one mentor. You have a series of mentors.

insights.claim: SMB Capital broadcasts its internal trader-development meetings (including reading-the-tape sessions with roughly 120 people listening) publicly for transparency, positioning this openness as a deliberate contrast to firms that operate behind closed doors.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Signals SMB's content/community strategy (open-access internal training as a recruiting and brand tool) — relevant context for evaluating the firm's public educational content as a genuine window into live decision-making rather than curated marketing.
insights.quote: We're sitting there with like, you know, call it 120 people and we're asking our traders to read the tape.

themes.theme: Recurring Market Patterns and Mental Models

insights.claim: Jeff's working heuristic for pattern recognition across different tickers and setups is that 'the market doesn't repeat, but it rhymes' — traders build the intuitive 'hits you between the eyes' recognition of a developing setup not because it looks identical to a past instance, but because it rhymes with previously studied, practiced patterns.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Explains why experienced discretionary traders can react quickly to novel-looking situations (like the CAR squeeze) — their edge is pattern-rhyming from deliberate practice, not exact pattern-matching, which argues for broad historical study over narrow backtesting.
insights.quote: The market doesn't repeat but it rhymes... you start to see it again and you're like oh yeah I kind of see the game that's being played here.

insights.claim: Jeff explicitly warns against acting on 'gut feel' trade ideas without running them through the firm's formal ASSET protocol, noting that every trader's gut talks to them constantly with plausible-sounding ideas, and that trading every gut signal would make him unprofitable.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: A concrete discipline check against the common trap of rationalizing impulsive trades as 'intuition' — intuition should generate hypotheses that then must clear a structured filter before risk is taken.
insights.quote: If I put risk on for every time my gut talked to me, I would not be a profitable trader because my gut talks to me all the time.

insights.claim: Jeff argues traders should habitually ask 'what would my trading look like if capital wasn't the constraint,' asserting that for most traders the real bottleneck to bigger results is capital/size access rather than skill.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Reframes a trader's growth bottleneck diagnosis toward capital access and firm/allocator relationships rather than assuming more strategy research is always the answer.
insights.quote: It's not skill holding them back. It's size.

insights.claim: The firm treats a trader's stated conviction level (verbalizing 'this is a B- setup' vs. 'this is an A+') as a real-time social/team signal — when one trader on the desk suddenly flags an A+ after a run of only C-grade ideas, it visibly raises attention and conviction among the rest of the team.
insights.speaker: Jeff Holden
insights.so_what: Shows how a shared, disciplined vocabulary for conviction (not just a private personal rule) creates a functional early-warning/attention system across a trading team.
insights.quote: If I say, 'Yeah, I just see a couple C opportunities and then all of a sudden I go I'm looking at this A+.' How much are the hairs in the back of your neck going to stand up when I say that?
